sections.h2: Where is Bridgeport, and who handles property tax there?
sections.html:
Bridgeport is the most populous city in Connecticut, with 148,654 residents in 2020, and it sits in eastern Fairfield County at the mouth of the Pequonnock River on Long Island Sound. The city is about 60 miles from Manhattan, and two City offices share the property tax work: the Tax Assessor values property and the Tax Collector bills and collects.

Bridgeport was incorporated as a town in 1821 and as a city in 1836. It runs under a mayor-council system. The city covers 19.4 square miles, of which 16.0 is land and 3.4 is water, and its elevation is only 3.3 feet, which matters for flood and storm questions later on this page.

TopicFact
Assessment dateOctober 1
Tax leviedThe following July 1
InstallmentsJuly 1 and January 1
Liens filedJune 30, the last day of the fiscal year
Real estate and personal property rate, 2026-202727.95 mills

sections.h2: How is Bridgeport property tax calculated?
sections.html:
Bridgeport multiplies the assessed value of a property by the mill rate, and one mill equals $1 of tax for each $1,000 of assessment. For fiscal year 2026-2027 the city's rate is 27.95 mills on real estate and personal property.

The city's own worked example uses an assessed value of $200,000. Multiplying $200,000 by 0.02795 gives a tax of $5,590. The city's example describes the figure as the 70 percent assessed value, which means the assessed value used for tax is a share of the market value and not the full market price.

That matters when you read your bill. The assessed value on the notice is the figure the mill rate applies to, so compare it with your bill rather than with a sale price.

The mill rate history is posted on the Tax Collector's general tax information page, and the Tax Assessor's page explains how taxes are determined.

sections.h2: When are Bridgeport property taxes due, and when do they go delinquent?
sections.html:
Bridgeport property tax is due in two installments, July 1 and January 1, and Connecticut law makes an installment delinquent if it is not paid by the first day of the next month. For the July installment that means August 1, and for the January installment it means February 1.

InstallmentDueDelinquent if unpaid after
FirstJuly 1August 1
SecondJanuary 1February 1

Under Connecticut General Statutes section 12-146, the delinquent part of the tax is charged interest at 18 percent a year from the date it was due. Each part of a month counts as a whole month, and the minimum interest charge is $2 per installment unless the municipality has voted not to impose it. Interest keeps running even after a judgment for the city.

The collector applies partial payments to interest first and principal second. A payment also counts as on time if it was made through a municipal electronic payment service in the allowed time or if the envelope carries a postmark within the allowed time.

The city files liens on June 30, the last day of the fiscal year, so ask the collector whether one has been filed against your property.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Bridgeport property assessment?
sections.html:
You appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals, and Connecticut law says the written appeal must be filed on or before February 20. The statute allows filing in writing or by email, in the manner the board prescribes.

The appeal has to include specific items:

  • The property owner's name and the signer's name and position.
  • A description of the property.
  • A name, mailing address and email address for all correspondence.
  • The reason for the appeal and your estimate of value.
  • The owner's or authorized agent's signature and the date.

The board must tell each filer the date, time and place of the hearing no later than March 1, and the notice has to go out at least seven calendar days before the hearing. For commercial, industrial, utility or apartment property assessed above $1 million, the board may choose not to hold a hearing, and in that case the owner can go straight to Superior Court under section 12-117a.

If the assessor received an extension, the filing deadline moves to March 20 and hearings take place in April. When the board changes a gross assessment, the new figure stays fixed until the next revaluation, with limited exceptions for new construction, damage, demolition, court orders and factual corrections.

A person who received title after the assessment date may also appeal, and so may a lessee bound by a recorded lease to pay the real property taxes. Ask the Tax Assessor's office for the current year's application form.

sections.h2: What is Bridgeport's history, and how did it shape the housing?
sections.html:
Bridgeport grew as a port and factory city, and by 1905 it was Connecticut's chief manufacturing city. Between 1870 and 1910 its population climbed from about 25,000 to more than 100,000, and many of those workers were immigrants from Ireland, Slovakia, Hungary, Germany, England and Italy.

P. T. Barnum lived in the city, served as mayor in 1871 and built four houses there. Harvey Hubbell founded Hubbell Incorporated in Bridgeport in 1888. After the Second World War the AVCO Lycoming division, founded in 1951, employed at times more than 12,000 people building military hardware, and it closed in 1984. Deindustrialization hit the city hard in the 1970s and 1980s.

Since the early 21st century the city has pursued large redevelopment projects. Its crime rate fell by nearly 50 percent between 2010 and 2018, according to the Wikipedia summary of the city.

This history explains why Bridgeport has a wide spread of housing ages and conditions. The city is also home to the University of Bridgeport, Housatonic Community College, part of Sacred Heart University, three museums and the state's only zoo.

sections.h2: Which parts of Bridgeport might a seller hear about?
sections.html:
Bridgeport is divided into five geographic areas, Downtown, the East Side, the North End, the South End and the West Side, and the city's neighborhood list is organized under those names. Each area has smaller neighborhoods inside it.

AreaNeighborhoods listed
DowntownMcLevy Green, Downtown South, Downtown North, The Hollow, Enterprise Zone
East SideSteel Point, Lower East Side, Upper East Side, East End, Boston Avenue/Mill Hill, Newfield, Pleasure Beach
North EndLake Forest, Lake Success, Reservoir/Whiskey Hill, Old Town Road, Brooklawn/Saint Vincent, Central End/Little Italy
South EndSeaside Park, Soundgate
West SideBlack Rock, West Side, West End, Saint Mary's by the Sea

The city calls itself the Park City because it has 35 public parks covering 1,300 acres. Sikorsky Memorial Airport serves the city, Route 8/25 runs toward Waterbury and Newtown, and Bridgeport Station serves commuter rail.

sections.h2: How do Bridgeport's climate and coastline affect a house?
sections.html:
Bridgeport's coastal location brings storm and flood questions that inland Connecticut towns face less often. Hurricanes and tropical storms have landed on the Connecticut coast in 1903, 1938, 1944, 1954, 1960, 1985 and, with Hurricane Sandy, in 2012.

The city averages 44.9 inches of precipitation a year and about 29 inches of snow, which is much less than inland Hartford or Albany. Snow cover of at least an inch lasts an average of 33 days each winter. The record low is 7 degrees below zero and the record high is 103 degrees.

For a seller, that history means a buyer, an insurer or a lender may ask whether the home sits in a flood zone, and it can matter for older basements, roofs and sea walls.

sections.h2: What should a Bridgeport seller do about unpaid property tax?
sections.html:
A seller with unpaid Bridgeport tax should get a payoff figure from the Tax Collector before closing, because interest at 18 percent a year keeps adding to a delinquent balance. A closing agent can pay the tax from the sale proceeds if the figure is current on the closing date.

  • List which installments are unpaid, July, January or both, and which fiscal years they belong to.
  • Ask for the interest to date and the per-month amount that will be added if closing slips.
  • Check whether a lien was filed on the last June 30.
  • If you think the assessment is wrong, the February 20 appeal date is a hard line, so do not wait until the closing is scheduled.

faqs.q: What is the Bridgeport mill rate?
faqs.a: For fiscal year 2026-2027 the city lists 27.95 mills for real estate and personal property and 31.75 mills for motor vehicles. One mill is $1 of tax per $1,000 of assessment.

faqs.q: When are Bridgeport property taxes due?
faqs.a: They are due in two installments, July 1 and January 1. Under state law an installment becomes delinquent if it is not paid by the first of the following month.

faqs.q: What interest does Bridgeport charge on late tax?
faqs.a: Connecticut General Statutes section 12-146 sets interest on the delinquent part at 18 percent a year, with a $2 minimum per installment unless the city votes not to impose it. Each part of a month counts as a whole month.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Bridgeport assessment?
faqs.a: The written appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals is due on or before February 20, or March 20 if the assessor was granted an extension.

faqs.q: Can a new owner appeal an assessment from before the purchase?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 12-111 lets a person to whom title was transferred since the assessment date appeal to the board.
